claim: Approximately 10–15% of the young to middle-aged adult population experience tinnitus.
source: Approximately 10–15% of the young to middle-aged adult population experience tinnitus as a common auditory phantom perception, with greater prevalence of 24% in older adults (Biswas et al., 2022; Henry et al., 2020; Jarach et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research (Biswas et al., 2022; Henry et al., 2020; Jarach et al., 2022).

claim: The prevalence of tinnitus is 24% in older adults.
source: Approximately 10–15% of the young to middle-aged adult population experience tinnitus as a common auditory phantom perception, with greater prevalence of 24% in older adults (Biswas et al., 2022; Henry et al., 2020; Jarach et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research (Biswas et al., 2022; Henry et al., 2020; Jarach et al., 2022).

claim: Bothersome tinnitus poses a significant detriment to quality of life due to reduced sleep quality, substantially increased distress, and anxiety.
source: For a smaller portion of the population, the sensation of bothersome tinnitus poses a significant detriment to quality of life, due to reduced sleep quality, substantially increased distress, and anxiety (Dobie, 2003) – all largely independent of the intensity or duration of the phantom perception (Kandeepan et al., 2019; Meyer et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research (Dobie, 2003; Kandeepan et al., 2019; Meyer et al., 2014).

claim: The detriment to quality of life from tinnitus is largely independent of the intensity or duration of the phantom perception.
source: For a smaller portion of the population, the sensation of bothersome tinnitus poses a significant detriment to quality of life, due to reduced sleep quality, substantially increased distress, and anxiety (Dobie, 2003) – all largely independent of the intensity or duration of the phantom perception (Kandeepan et al., 2019; Meyer et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research (Kandeepan et al., 2019; Meyer et al., 2014).

claim: Hearing loss has been identified as a main risk factor for tinnitus.
source: Hearing loss has been identified as a main risk factor for tinnitus (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research (Kim et al., 2015).

claim: For 75–80% of people with tinnitus, objective audiometric testing indicates hearing loss.
source: Indeed, for 75–80% of people with tinnitus, objective audiometric testing indicates hearing loss (Wallhäusser-Franke et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research (Wallhäusser-Franke et al., 2017).

claim: Some form of auditory damage – even without clear audiometric changes – facilitates tinnitus development.
source: Previous findings support the idea that some form of auditory damage – even without clear audiometric changes – facilitates tinnitus development (Roberts et al., 2006; Schaette and McAlpine, 2011; Schaette et al., 2012; Weisz et al., 2006) and provokes maladaptive changes.
evidence: Supported by citations to published research (Roberts et al., 2006; Schaette and McAlpine, 2011; Schaette et al., 2012; Weisz et al., 2006).

claim: Increased neural activity following hearing loss has been observed in animal models.
source: Based on the observation of increased neural activity following hearing loss in animal models (Eggermont and Roberts, 2004; Roberts et al., 2010), a still-influential 'altered-gain' view holds that reduced auditory input following hearing damage leads neurons in the auditory pathway to increase their responsivity, thereby restoring their mean activity level; in this framework, the perception of phantom sounds is a 'downside' to this homeostatic process, as spontaneous activity can engage downstream auditory regions (Schaette and Kempter, 2006; Sedley, 2019a).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research (Eggermont and Roberts, 2004; Roberts et al., 2010).

claim: The 'altered-gain' view holds that reduced auditory input following hearing damage leads neurons in the auditory pathway to increase their responsivity, thereby restoring their mean activity level.
source: Based on the observation of increased neural activity following hearing loss in animal models (Eggermont and Roberts, 2004; Roberts et al., 2010), a still-influential 'altered-gain' view holds that reduced auditory input following hearing damage leads neurons in the auditory pathway to increase their responsivity, thereby restoring their mean activity level; in this framework, the perception of phantom sounds is a 'downside' to this homeostatic process, as spontaneous activity can engage downstream auditory regions (Schaette and Kempter, 2006; Sedley, 2019a).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research (Schaette and Kempter, 2006; Sedley, 2019a).

claim: In the 'altered-gain' framework, the perception of phantom sounds is a 'downside' to the homeostatic process, as spontaneous activity can engage downstream auditory regions.
source: Based on the observation of increased neural activity following hearing loss in animal models (Eggermont and Roberts, 2004; Roberts et al., 2010), a still-influential 'altered-gain' view holds that reduced auditory input following hearing damage leads neurons in the auditory pathway to increase their responsivity, thereby restoring their mean activity level; in this framework, the perception of phantom sounds is a 'downside' to this homeostatic process, as spontaneous activity can engage downstream auditory regions (Schaette and Kempter, 2006; Sedley, 2019a).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research (Schaette and Kempter, 2006; Sedley, 2019a).

claim: Empirical support for tinnitus frameworks in humans is weak, difficult to replicate, and marked by strong interindividual variability.
source: However, apart from a significant shortage of data bridging animal and human research in these different frameworks, empirical support in humans is weak, difficult to replicate, and marked by strong interindividual variability (Eggermont and Roberts, 2015; Elgoyhen et al., 2015; Reisinger et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research (Eggermont and Roberts, 2015; Elgoyhen et al., 2015; Reisinger et al., 2023).

claim: People with hearing loss do not necessarily experience tinnitus.
source: Beyond the lack of solid evidence, the models face further explanatory challenges (Sedley, 2019a): (1) People with hearing loss do not necessarily experience tinnitus (Wallhäusser-Franke et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research (Wallhäusser-Franke et al., 2017).

claim: The onsets of tinnitus and hearing loss often do not occur at the same time.
source: (2) The onsets of tinnitus and hearing loss often do not occur at the same time (Roberts et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research (Roberts et al., 2010).

claim: Not all cases of acute tinnitus transform into chronic tinnitus.
source: (3) Not all cases of acute tinnitus transform into chronic tinnitus (Mühlmeier et al., 2016; Vielsmeier et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research (Mühlmeier et al., 2016; Vielsmeier et al., 2020).

claim: A Bayesian inference framework for tinnitus perception has been developed.
source: One attempt along these lines has been the development of a Bayesian inference framework for tinnitus perception (Sedley et al., 2016a).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research (Sedley et al., 2016a).

claim: The Bayesian inference framework emphasizes the constructive nature of perception being guided by internal models.
source: This framework emphasizes the constructive nature of perception being guided by internal models (Helmholtz, 1867).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research (Helmholtz, 1867).

claim: In the Bayesian framework, sensory input is dynamically compared to predictions or so-called priors.
source: Therein, sensory input is dynamically compared to predictions or so-called priors.
evidence: Based on established predictive coding theory.

claim: The Bayesian framework holds that spontaneous activity in the auditory pathway acts as a precursor of tinnitus.
source: The framework holds that spontaneous activity in the auditory pathway acts as a precursor of tinnitus.
evidence: Based on the Bayesian inference framework for tinnitus.

claim: In the healthy auditory system, spontaneous activity is 'ignored', due to the default prior of silence.
source: In the healthy auditory system, spontaneous activity is 'ignored', due to the default prior of silence.
evidence: Based on the Bayesian inference framework for tinnitus.

claim: Certain circumstances can shift the prior of silence, such that a particular sound is expected.
source: However, certain circumstances can shift this prior, such that a particular sound is expected (Hullfish et al., 2019; Sedley et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research (Hullfish et al., 2019; Sedley et al., 2016b).

claim: Few studies have provided support for altered prediction processes in tinnitus using EEG evoked responses.
source: Few studies have provided support for altered prediction processes in tinnitus, which is in line with the predictive-coding framework using either EEG evoked responses (Mohan et al., 2022; Sedley et al., 2019b) or computational modeling (Hu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research (Mohan et al., 2022; Sedley et al., 2019b).

claim: Few studies have provided support for altered prediction processes in tinnitus using computational modeling.
source: Few studies have provided support for altered prediction processes in tinnitus, which is in line with the predictive-coding framework using either EEG evoked responses (Mohan et al., 2022; Sedley et al., 2019b) or computational modeling (Hu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research (Hu et al., 2021).

claim: In Study 1, 34 individuals with tinnitus participated in the experiment.
source: In Study 1, a total of 34 individuals with tinnitus (17 females, age 20–67 years, mean = 45.12, sd = 13.65) participated in the experiment.
evidence: Direct statement of participant numbers in Study 1.

claim: In Study 1, 25 individuals with tinnitus were age-matched with the control group and used for group comparisons.
source: Within this group, 25 individuals (16 females, age 20–66 years, mean = 40.92, sd = 13.17) were age-matched (in all cases but one both age- and sex-matched) with the control group and used for group comparisons.
evidence: Direct statement of matched participant numbers in Study 1.

claim: In Study 1, standardized pure-tone audiometric testing for frequencies from 125 Hz to 8 kHz was performed in 31 out of 34 tinnitus participants.
source: Standardized pure-tone audiometric testing for frequencies from 125 Hz to 8 kHz was performed in 31 out of 34 tinnitus participants using Interacoustic AS608 audiometer.
evidence: Direct statement of audiometric testing in Study 1.

claim: In Study 1, 25 individuals reporting no relevant audiological, neurological or psychiatric treatment history took part as a control group.
source: 25 individuals (16 females, age 21–65 years, mean = 41.56, sd = 13.68) reporting no relevant audiological, neurological or psychiatric treatment history took part as a control group.
evidence: Direct statement of control group characteristics in Study 1.

claim: In Study 1, no differences were shown for age between the tinnitus and control samples.
source: No differences were shown for age between the samples (t = 0.17, p = 0.89).
evidence: Statistical test result showing no age difference in Study 1.

claim: In Study 1, pure-tone audiometric testing was not included for the control subjects, so group comparisons between hearing thresholds were not feasible.
source: As pure-tone audiometric testing was not included for the control subjects, group comparisons between hearing thresholds were not feasible.
evidence: Direct statement of methodological limitation in Study 1.

claim: In Study 2, 40 individuals with tinnitus and 40 hearing-, age-, and sex-matched control subjects completed the experiment.
source: In Study 2, 40 individuals with tinnitus (16 females, age 24–74 years, mean = 57.73, sd = 14.12), as well as 40 hearing-, age-, and sex-matched control subjects (16 females, age 24–76 years, mean = 57.43, sd = 13.94) completed the experiment.
evidence: Direct statement of participant numbers and matching in Study 2.

claim: In Study 2, inclusion criteria for the tinnitus group were a tinnitus duration of more than 6 months.
source: For the tinnitus group, inclusion criteria were a tinnitus duration of more than 6 months.
evidence: Direct statement of inclusion criteria in Study 2.

claim: In Study 2, no participants with psychiatric or neurological diseases were included in the sample.
source: No participants with psychiatric or neurological diseases were included in the sample.
evidence: Direct statement of exclusion criteria in Study 2.

claim: In Study 2, hearing loss was defined by a hearing threshold higher than 30 dB HL in at least one frequency.
source: We also performed pure-tone audiometric testing and defined hearing loss by a hearing threshold higher than 30 dB HL in at least one frequency.
evidence: Direct statement of hearing loss definition in Study 2.

claim: In Study 2, four individuals with tinnitus did not show any audiometric abnormality.
source: Four individuals with tinnitus did not show any audiometric abnormality; four of the participants showed unilateral hearing impairments on at least one frequency; 26 volunteers had high-frequency hearing loss (i.e. hearing thresholds higher than 30 dB); and six individuals were hearing impaired over most frequencies (i.e. hearing thresholds higher than 30 dB).
evidence: Direct statement of audiometric findings in Study 2.

claim: In Study 2, no differences in hearing status over frequencies between groups were found for the left ear.
source: Using independent t-tests, we found no differences in hearing status over frequencies between groups for the left (t = −1.19, p = 0.238) and right ear (t = −1.72, p = 0.09).
evidence: Statistical test result showing no hearing difference in Study 2.

claim: In Study 2, no differences in hearing status over frequencies between groups were found for the right ear.
source: Using independent t-tests, we found no differences in hearing status over frequencies between groups for the left (t = −1.19, p = 0.238) and right ear (t = −1.72, p = 0.09).
evidence: Statistical test result showing no hearing difference in Study 2.

claim: In Study 2, a linear regression showed that hearing thresholds did not differ between ears and groups, but solely between frequencies.
source: An additional linear regression including all frequencies from 125 to 8000 Hz also showed that hearing thresholds did not differ between ears (b = 0.311, SE = 1.600, p = 0.846) and groups (b = 1.702, SE = 1.553, p = 0.273), but solely between frequencies (b = 0.003, SE = 0.000, p < 0.001).
evidence: Statistical test result from linear regression in Study 2.

claim: In Study 1, four different pure tones were presented, with carrier frequencies logarithmically spaced between 200 and 2000 Hz.
source: In Study 1, four different pure (sinusoidal) tones were presented, with carrier frequencies logarithmically spaced between 200 and 2000 Hz (200, 431, 928, and 2000 Hz) analogous to the original paradigm (Demarchi et al., 2019).
evidence: Direct statement of stimulus parameters in Study 1.

claim: In Study 2, carrier frequencies of the four tones were logarithmically spaced between approximately 440 and 1043 Hz.
source: In Study 2, carrier frequencies of the four tones were logarithmically spaced between approximately 440 and 1043 Hz (i.e. 440, 587, 782, and 1043 Hz).
evidence: Direct statement of stimulus parameters in Study 2.

claim: In both Study 1 and Study 2, each tone lasted 100 ms, tapered at both ends with 5 ms linearly ascending/descending periods.
source: In both designs, each tone lasted 100 ms, tapered at both ends with 5 ms linearly ascending/descending periods, and we presented the sounds at a constant 3-Hz stimulation rate.
evidence: Direct statement of stimulus parameters in both studies.

claim: In both Study 1 and Study 2, sounds were presented at a constant 3-Hz stimulation rate.
source: In both designs, each tone lasted 100 ms, tapered at both ends with 5 ms linearly ascending/descending periods, and we presented the sounds at a constant 3-Hz stimulation rate.
evidence: Direct statement of stimulus parameters in both studies.

claim: In Study 1, four blocks of tone sequences comprising 4000 stimuli were presented, each lasting approximately 22 min.
source: In Study 1, we presented four blocks of tone sequences comprising 4000 stimuli, each lasting approximately 22 min.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design in Study 1.

claim: In Study 1, four entropy conditions were used for the design.
source: We used four entropy conditions for the design.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design in Study 1.

claim: In Study 1, the random condition had the highest entropy (i.e. the lowest regularity), and the transition probabilities from one sound to another were equal.
source: The random condition had the highest entropy (i.e. the lowest regularity), and the transition probabilities from one sound to another were equal, preventing any possibility of accurately predicting upcoming stimuli.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design in Study 1.

claim: In Study 1, the ordered condition had the lowest entropy level (i.e. the highest regularity), and in 75% of trials, one sound was followed by a specific other sound.
source: In contrast, the ordered condition had the lowest entropy level (i.e. the highest regularity), and in 75% of trials, one sound was followed by a specific other sound. In 25% of trials, the same sound was repeated.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design in Study 1.

claim: In Study 1, a randomly chosen 10% of the sounds were omitted in all conditions.
source: Furthermore, a randomly chosen 10% of the sounds were omitted in all conditions (not included in the current analysis), resulting in 900 sound trials and 100 omission trials per entropy block, that is 3600 sounds and 400 omissions in total.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design in Study 1.

claim: In Study 2, no omissions were included, and participants solely listened to sounds that were either random or ordered.
source: Furthermore, no omissions were included, and participants solely listened to sounds that were either random or ordered.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design in Study 2.

claim: In Study 2, data collection comprised 1500 stimuli of each condition.
source: Therefore, data collection comprised 1500 stimuli of each condition.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design in Study 2.

claim: Magnetic brain activity was measured using a whole-head MEG with 102 magnetometers and 204 orthogonally placed planar gradiometers.
source: We measured magnetic brain activity using a whole-head MEG (Triux, MEGIN Oy, Finland), in which brain signals were captured by 102 magnetometers and 204 orthogonally placed planar gradiometers.
evidence: Direct statement of MEG data acquisition parameters.

claim: MEG data was sampled at a rate of 1000 Hz.
source: Participants sat in a dimly lit magnetically shielded room (AK3b, Vacuumschmelze, Germany) and were measured with a sampling rate of 1000 Hz and default hardware filters set by the manufacturer (0.1 Hz high pass to 330 Hz low pass).
evidence: Direct statement of MEG data acquisition parameters.

claim: In Study 1, both tinnitus and control groups exhibited a rapid increase of decoding accuracy following sound onset.
source: Both groups exhibited a rapid increase of decoding accuracy following sound onset, robustly observed at an individual level (Figure 2).

claim: In Study 1, above chance decoding accuracy started immediately after stimulus onset in both groups.

source: A second, negative cluster (p = 0.05) between 360 and 800 ms was observed, caused by inverse tendencies for the tinnitus and control groups (Figure 3A): that is, whereas individuals with tinnitus appeared to quickly deactivate carrier-frequency patterns the more regular the sound sequence became, control individuals reactivate patterns of the decoded sound presented at sound onset upon presentation of new events.
evidence: Statistical test result shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In Study 1, individuals with tinnitus appeared to quickly deactivate carrier-frequency patterns the more regular the sound sequence became.
source: A second, negative cluster (p = 0.05) between 360 and 800 ms was observed, caused by inverse tendencies for the tinnitus and control groups (Figure 3A): that is, whereas individuals with tinnitus appeared to quickly deactivate carrier-frequency patterns the more regular the sound sequence became, control individuals reactivate patterns of the decoded sound presented at sound onset upon presentation of new events.

evidence: Observation from data analysis shown in Figure 3A.

source: We further averaged the time courses of β-coefficients over the training time of 450–550 ms after stimulus onset which showed that whereas individuals with tinnitus exhibited relatively stable processing in the pre-sound period, results for control individuals were marked by a weaker processing the more regular the sound sequences were (captured by the negative β-coefficients, Figure 3B).
evidence: Observation from data analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In Study 1, results for control individuals were marked by a weaker processing the more regular the sound sequences were.
source: We further averaged the time courses of β-coefficients over the training time of 450–550 ms after stimulus onset which showed that whereas individuals with tinnitus exhibited relatively stable processing in the pre-sound period, results for control individuals were marked by a weaker processing the more regular the sound sequences were (captured by the negative β-coefficients, Figure 3B).

source: Despite the explorative (liberal) testing without multiple comparison corrections, no significant correlation effects were identified for the pre-stimulus positive cluster for hearing thresholds (rho = −0.06, p = 0.75), tinnitus loudness (rho = −0.06, p = 0.73), and tinnitus distress (rho = 0.11, p = 0.53).
evidence: Statistical test result from correlation analysis in Study 1.

claim: In Study 1, no significant correlation was found between β-regression values and tinnitus distress in the tinnitus sample.
source: Despite the explorative (liberal) testing without multiple comparison corrections, no significant correlation effects were identified for the pre-stimulus positive cluster for hearing thresholds (rho = −0.06, p = 0.75), tinnitus loudness (rho = −0.06, p = 0.73), and tinnitus distress (rho = 0.11, p = 0.53).
evidence: Statistical test result from correlation analysis in Study 1.

claim: In Study 2, decoding performance peaked at ~100 ms for the entire sample.
source: As illustrated in Figure 4A (red line), this is clearly the case for the entire sample (t260 = 8.40, 95% CI [0.0092, 0.0148], p < 0.001), with a rapid increase of decoding performance peaking at ~100 ms, and a slow decrease however with above chance decoding performance lasting throughout the entire post-stimulus period, including a small increase following the subsequent tone presented at 333 ms.
evidence: Statistical test result shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In Study 2, above chance decoding performance lasted throughout the entire post-stimulus period.
source: As illustrated in Figure 4A (red line), this is clearly the case for the entire sample (t260 = 8.40, 95% CI [0.0092, 0.0148], p < 0.001), with a rapid increase of decoding performance peaking at ~100 ms, and a slow decrease however with above chance decoding performance lasting throughout the entire post-stimulus period, including a small increase following the subsequent tone presented at 333 ms.
evidence: Statistical test result shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In Study 2, source analyses demonstrated strong activations in the temporal areas in both hemispheres for the first time window.
source: Consecutive source analyses demonstrated strong activations in the temporal areas in both hemispheres for the first time window which were still present in the later time window – however less pronounced and more lateralized (Figure 4B).

claim: Comparing Study 1 and Study 2, a ~30 ms delay can be seen in Study 2.
source: However, when comparing the outcomes of both studies, some differences can be noticed. First, a ~30 ms delay can be seen in Study 2 and more importantly, accuracies were significantly lower (t260 = 2.16, 95% CI [0.0005, 0.0109], p = 0.031).

claim: Comparing Study 1 and Study 2, decoding accuracies were significantly lower in Study 2.
source: However, when comparing the outcomes of both studies, some differences can be noticed. First, a ~30 ms delay can be seen in Study 2 and more importantly, accuracies were significantly lower (t260 = 2.16, 95% CI [0.0005, 0.0109], p = 0.031).
evidence: Statistical test result comparing Study 1 and Study 2.

claim: In Study 2, one-sided cluster-based permutation t-tests revealed a significant positive cluster when testing on the pre-stimulus interval between –400 and 0 ms.
source: To focus our analysis on the replication we targeted a 470- to 570-ms time window for training, which yielded the strongest effect in Study 1. When testing on the pre-stimulus interval between –400 and 0 ms, one-sided cluster-based permutation t-tests revealed a significant positive cluster (tsum = 26.2, p = 0.046).
evidence: Statistical test result from Study 2.

claim: In Study 2, the significant positive cluster indicated relatively higher decoding accuracies in the tinnitus group.
source: In line with our prediction, this indicated relatively higher decoding accuracies in the tinnitus group and therefore replicated the central finding in Study 1 (Figure 6A).
evidence: Interpretation of statistical test result shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In Study 2, the effect appeared to be most pronounced in the time window between –410 and –310 ms.
source: The effect appeared to be most pronounced in the time window between –410 and –310 ms. In this time frame, relevant t-values ranged from t = 1.90 to t = 2.75 with significant p-values between p = 0.005 and p = 0.036, indicating stronger differences in decoding accuracy between ordered and random sound sequences (i.e. higher prediction scores) in the tinnitus group.
evidence: Statistical test result from Study 2.

claim: In Study 2, prediction scores in the tinnitus group did not significantly vary from zero.
source: Comparing the prediction scores against zero within each group indicated non-significance for the tinnitus group with t78 = 0.063, 95% CI [–0.0017, 0.0018], p = 0.950.
evidence: Statistical test result from Study 2.

claim: In Study 2, prediction scores in the control group significantly varied from zero.
source: In the group without tinnitus, however, prediction scores significantly varied from zero (t78 = −3.65, 95% CI [–0.0047, –0.0014], p < .001).
evidence: Statistical test result from Study 2.

claim: In Study 2, prediction score differences between tinnitus and control groups are driven by below-chance accuracy in the control group at late training time intervals.
source: This indeed indicates that prediction score differences between tinnitus and control groups are driven by below-chance accuracy in the control group at these late training time intervals.
evidence: Interpretation of statistical test results from Study 2.

claim: In Study 2, averaged over time, no significant difference between the participants with and without tinnitus was observed for decoding accuracy in the random condition.
source: Results showed that, averaged over time, no significant difference between the participants with and without tinnitus was observed using an independent sample t-tests (t260 = 0.795, 95% CI [–0.0024, 0.0056], p = 0.428).
evidence: Statistical test result from Study 2.

claim: In Study 2, an equivalence test yielded a significant result, indicating equivalence between the tinnitus and control groups for decoding accuracy in the random condition.
source: As absence of evidence does not equal evidence of absence of an effect, we included an additional equivalence test (Walker and Nowacki, 2011). This yielded a significant result of t73.93 = −19.08, p < 0.001, indicating equivalence between the two groups (Figure 6C).
evidence: Statistical test result shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In Study 2, Spearman's rank correlation revealed no significant relation between tinnitus distress and decoding accuracy.
source: Thus, building on our previous study, Spearman's rank correlation revealed no significant relation between tinnitus distress and decoding accuracy with r(30) = 0.25, p = 0.168 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Statistical test result shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Tinnitus distress values assessed by the mini-TQ did not differ significantly between Studies 1 and 2.
source: We additionally compared tinnitus distress values assessed by the mini-TQ (Goebel and Hiller, 1992) between Studies 1 and 2 to detect potential differences between the samples, however, results of the Welch's t-test were not significant with t(30.7) = 1.27, p = 0.214.
evidence: Statistical test result comparing Studies 1 and 2.

claim: Bayes factors demonstrated relevant effects in both datasets in the pre-stimulus interval at around –400 ms, however, values are much higher in Study 1 as compared to Study 2 (maximum BF 120.7 vs 7.4).
source: Bayes factors demonstrated relevant effects in both datasets in the pre-stimulus interval at around –400 ms, however, values are much higher in Study 1 as compared to Study 2 (maximum BF 120.7 vs 7.4).
evidence: Bayes factor analysis comparing Study 1 and Study 2.

claim: In Study 1, Bayes factors greater than 3 were solely found for subsets with higher numbers of trials (i.e. 3600 or 1500 trials).
source: These values were solely found for subsets with higher numbers of trials (i.e. 3600 or 1500 trials). A lower number of trials like 750 or 200 trials showed no relevant group differences.
evidence: Bayes factor analysis of trial number effects in Study 1.

claim: The number of trials highly impacts the strength of effects.
source: Therefore, the number of trials highly impacts the strength of effects and was likely responsible for the smaller effects in Study 2 since solely 1500 trials per condition were included.
evidence: Inference from Bayes factor analysis of trial number effects.

claim: In Study 2, prediction scores significantly predicted whether participants experience tinnitus.

evidence: Speculative interpretation based on predictive coding theory.

claim: In tinnitus, sensitivity to predictable stimuli could be enhanced.
source: In tinnitus, this sensitivity to predictable stimuli could therefore be enhanced.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of findings.

claim: People with a tinnitus predisposition are less likely to suppress a signal on account of its predictabilities, and therefore that signal is more likely to become perceptible initially.
source: People with a tinnitus predisposition are less likely to suppress that signal on account of its predictabilities, and therefore that signal is more likely to become perceptible initially.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of findings.

claim: Downregulations of higher-level auditory processes for predicted stimuli can indicate that auditory predictions become more strongly represented, and therefore harder to change through competing sensory evidence.
source: Downregulations of higher-level auditory processes for predicted stimuli can then indicate that auditory predictions become more strongly represented, and therefore harder to change through competing sensory evidence.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of findings.

claim: Fundamental differences in auditory processing 'styles' could be an interesting conceptual bridge to addressing why tinnitus becomes chronic and so therapy resistant in some individuals.
source: These fundamental differences in auditory processing 'styles' could also be an interesting conceptual bridge to addressing why tinnitus becomes chronic and so therapy resistant in some individuals.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of findings.

claim: The interpretations of the below-chance decoding remain speculative at this stage and requires further investigation.
source: As indicated above, these interpretations remain speculative at this stage and requires further investigation.
evidence: Acknowledgment of speculative nature of interpretations.

claim: There are other possibilities on how to interpret the below-chance decoding.
source: We acknowledge that there are other possibilities on how to interpret the below-chance decoding and therefore encourage future work to implement novel approaches to gain more insights into the exact underlying mechanisms driving this effect.
evidence: Acknowledgment of alternative interpretations.

claim: An increased focus on hippocampal regions could be a worthwhile complement to MEG work, given the outstanding relevance of medial temporal areas in the formation of associations in statistical learning paradigms.
source: An increased focus on hippocampal regions, for example, in fMRI, patient, or animal studies, could be a worthwhile complement to our MEG work, given the outstanding relevance of medial temporal areas in the formation of associations in statistical learning paradigms (see e.g. Covington et al., 2018; Paquette et al., 2017; Schapiro et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculation about future research directions with citations (Covington et al., 2018; Paquette et al., 2017; Schapiro et al., 2016).

claim: Despite the successful replication of core findings in Study 2, group differences effects were weaker compared to Study 1.
source: Despite the successful replication of our core findings in Study 2, it is noticeable that group differences effects were weaker compared to Study 1.
evidence: Comparison of effect sizes between studies.

claim: Understanding which aspects contribute to the decline in effect size is relevant for future works.
source: Understanding which aspects contribute to this decline in effect size is relevant for future works.
evidence: Statement about the importance of understanding effect size differences.

claim: The control for hearing loss leading to a decrease in the magnitude of the effect is deemed very unlikely.
source: An obvious assumption could be that the control for hearing loss led to a decrease in the magnitude of the effect. Even though this possibility cannot be completely excluded, we deem it very unlikely as hearing loss was neither associated with the prediction score in Study 1 (audiometry was available for the tinnitus group) nor in Study 2 assessed in the logistic regression analysis.
evidence: Inference from correlation and regression analyses.

claim: Closer frequencies lead to more similar neural patterns hence making it more challenging for a classifier to decode tone frequencies.
source: However, closer frequencies lead to more similar neural patterns hence making it more challenging for a classifier to decode tone frequencies.
evidence: Based on principles of neural coding and classification.

claim: The lower decoding accuracy for carrier frequencies and slightly shifted decoding peaks in the random sequence in Study 2 are a testimony to the issue of closer frequencies.
source: The lower decoding accuracy for carrier frequencies and slightly shifted decoding peaks in the random sequence in Study 2 are a testimony to this issue.
evidence: Observation from data comparison between studies.

claim: Less reliable decoding in Study 2 likely obscured group differences to some extent.
source: As these classifiers were also applied to the pre-stimulus periods of the ordered sequence, less reliable decoding likely obscured group differences to some extent.
evidence: Inference about the impact of decoding accuracy on group differences.

claim: Study 2 included 1500 trials per carrier frequency, which is likely on the boundary of finding predefined group effects.
source: Study 2 included 1500 trials per carrier frequency, which is likely on the boundary of finding predefined group effects.
evidence: Inference from trial number analysis.

claim: Both studies used individual sound intensity levels to ensure a comfortable listening situation for the participants.
source: Third, both studies used individual sound intensity levels to ensure a comfortable listening situation for the participants.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental procedure.

claim: Differences in sound intensity levels are a potential confound in the experimental design as sound intensity can have an impact on neural responses.
source: These differences in sound intensity levels are, however, a potential confound in the experimental design as well since sound intensity can have an impact on neural responses (Thaerig et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research (Thaerig et al., 2008).

claim: The authors are not able to ultimately exclude the sound intensity level as a driver of the effects.
source: Although in this design, we expect the intensity levels balanced equally to the hearing loss of the participants (which did not differ between groups), and basic decoding of sound frequency did not differ in both studies, we are not able to ultimately exclude the sound intensity level as a driver of our effects.
evidence: Acknowledgment of potential confound.

claim: Future studies should include a perceived loudness matching for each frequency and should compare the adapted sound intensity values between each group or integrate them into the analysis.
source: Future studies should include a perceived loudness matching for each frequency and should compare the adapted sound intensity values between each group or integrate them into the analysis (e.g. using the logistic regression approach in Figure 8).
evidence: Recommendation for future research.

claim: The work clearly underlines the true presence of differences, in terms of predictive processing, between individuals with and without tinnitus.
source: Overall, our work clearly underlines the true presence of differences, in terms of predictive processing, between individuals with and without tinnitus.
evidence: Summary of findings from both studies.

claim: Distinct design choices impact the strength of the effects.
source: At the same time, distinct design choices impact the strength of the effects which is not only apparent in the present work but was also reported recently by Yukhnovich et al., 2024.
evidence: Inference from current work and citation to published research (Yukhnovich et al., 2024).

claim: Future studies using the paradigm and analysis approach should opt for a broad frequency spacing (>2 octaves) and ideally more than 2000 trials per carrier frequency in the random sequence.
source: Further to controlling for basic variables (age, sex, and hearing loss), future studies using our paradigm and analysis approach should opt for a broad frequency spacing (>2 octaves) and ideally more than 2000 trials per carrier frequency in the random sequence.
evidence: Recommendation based on findings from both studies.

claim: The recommendations for future studies are likely even more important for efforts of testing this paradigm using EEG, which normally comes with inferior data quality as compared to MEG.
source: These recommendations are likely even more important for efforts of testing this paradigm using EEG, which normally comes with inferior data quality as compared to MEG.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about EEG vs MEG data quality.

claim: Attention appears to be relevant in tinnitus, both in the generation and the formation of predictions.
source: Furthermore, apart from the methodological specifications mentioned above, attention appears to be relevant in tinnitus as well, both in the generation and the formation of predictions (Durai et al., 2018; Roberts et al., 2013; Sedley et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research (Durai et al., 2018; Roberts et al., 2013; Sedley et al., 2016b).

claim: In the current work, passive listening tasks including a movie were used to reduce attentional focus on the presented stimuli.
source: In the current work, we used passive listening tasks including a movie to reduce attentional focus on the presented stimuli.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental procedure.

claim: The authors cannot draw conclusions whether differences in attention had an influence on the effects.
source: Therefore, we cannot draw conclusions whether differences in attention had an influence on the effects.
evidence: Acknowledgment of limitation.

claim: Future studies should include more manipulations of attention to investigate its relevance.
source: Future studies should include more manipulations of attention to investigate its relevance.
evidence: Recommendation for future research.

claim: Pure-tone audiometric testing in Study 2 was solely performed up to 8 kHz.
source: Additionally, we rigorously controlled for hearing loss in Study 2, however, pure-tone audiometric testing was solely performed up to 8 kHz and we were therefore not able to draw conclusions regarding hearing impairments in higher frequencies and their influence on the effects.
evidence: Direct statement of methodological limitation.

claim: The authors were not able to draw conclusions regarding hearing impairments in higher frequencies and their influence on the effects.
source: Additionally, we rigorously controlled for hearing loss in Study 2, however, pure-tone audiometric testing was solely performed up to 8 kHz and we were therefore not able to draw conclusions regarding hearing impairments in higher frequencies and their influence on the effects.
evidence: Acknowledgment of limitation.

claim: The authors did not screen participants for hyperacusis.
source: Moreover, we did not screen our participants for hyperacusis.
evidence: Direct statement of methodological limitation.

claim: Hyperacusis is widely correlated with the sensation of tinnitus and underlying neural mechanisms are potentially intertwined with tinnitus processes.
source: This hypersensitivity to mild sounds is widely correlated with the sensation of tinnitus and underlying neural mechanisms are potentially intertwined with tinnitus processes (Schilling et al., 2023; Yukhnovich et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research (Schilling et al., 2023; Yukhnovich et al., 2023).

claim: Screening for hyperacusis in future work can reveal more details on participant characteristics influencing predictive processing.
source: Screening for hyperacusis in future work can therefore reveal more details on participant characteristics influencing predictive processing.
evidence: Recommendation for future research.

claim: In both studies, tinnitus distress was not correlated with the reported prediction effects.
source: In both studies, tinnitus distress was not correlated with the reported prediction effects.
evidence: Summary of correlation analysis results from both studies.

claim: Tinnitus can be characterized by other features such as its loudness, pitch or duration which were not included in the experimental assessment.
source: Nevertheless, tinnitus can also be characterized by other features such as its loudness, pitch or duration which were not included in the experimental assessment.
evidence: Acknowledgment of limitation.

claim: The authors solely used a short version of the Mini-TQ in Study 2, which did not allow relating prediction scores to subscales like sleep disturbances.
source: Additionally, we solely used a short version of the Mini-TQ (Goebel and Hiller, 1992) in Study 2, which did not allow us to relate prediction scores to subscales like sleep disturbances which potentially influence cognitive functioning and thus predictive processing.
evidence: Acknowledgment of limitation with citation (Goebel and Hiller, 1992).

claim: Sleep disturbances potentially influence cognitive functioning and thus predictive processing.
source: Additionally, we solely used a short version of the Mini-TQ (Goebel and Hiller, 1992) in Study 2, which did not allow us to relate prediction scores to subscales like sleep disturbances which potentially influence cognitive functioning and thus predictive processing.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about sleep and cognition.

claim: Tinnitus is often accompanied by psychological comorbidities such as depression or anxiety which are potential confounds of the results.
source: Next to sleeping disorders and distress, tinnitus is often also accompanied by psychological comorbidities such as depression or anxiety (Langguth, 2011) which are potential confounds of the results.
evidence: Supported by citation to published research (Langguth, 2011).

claim: For the work described in this manuscript the replicability of the core finding was of main importance.
source: For the work described in this manuscript the replicability of the core finding was of main importance.
evidence: Statement of research priority.

claim: More studies are needed to relate the prediction patterns in more detail to aspects of tinnitus sensation and distress.
source: More studies are needed taking into account to assess relate the prediction patterns in more detail to aspects of tinnitus sensation and distress.
evidence: Recommendation for future research.

claim: The present work poses the rare instance of a replicable effect in the human neuroscientific tinnitus literature.
source: The present work poses the rare instance of a replicable effect in the human neuroscientific tinnitus literature, particularly of the core effect of an enhanced prediction score in tinnitus.
evidence: Summary of the significance of findings.

claim: The results of Study 2 bear particular relevance by excluding hearing loss as a confounding explanation for the observed differences in anticipatory neural information in tinnitus.
source: The results of Study 2 bear particular relevance by excluding hearing loss as a confounding explanation for the observed differences in anticipatory neural information in tinnitus.
evidence: Summary of Study 2 contribution.

claim: The robustness of the effect despite changes of some design details is worth emphasizing.
source: Bolstered by the recommendation as a registered report, the robustness of the effect despite changes of some design details is worth emphasizing.
evidence: Summary of the significance of replication.

claim: The narrower frequency range in the pre-registered second study showed that the effects are to some extent generalizable and not bound to higher-frequency falling into a tinnitus-frequency range.
source: For example, the narrower frequency range in the pre-registered second study showed that the effects are to some extent generalizable and not bound to for example, higher-frequency falling into a tinnitus-frequency range.
evidence: Inference from design differences and replication.

claim: Some of the design details likely had an adverse impact on the effect size.
source: However, some of the design details likely had an adverse impact on the effect size.
evidence: Inference from comparison of effect sizes.

claim: Concrete suggestions for future studies using the paradigm have been offered.
source: Concrete suggestions for future studies using our paradigm have been offered.
evidence: Summary of recommendations provided.

claim: The core pre-stimulus predictive processing effect is caused by a below-chance decoding accuracy in the non-tinnitus group.
source: We concluded that the core pre-stimulus predictive processing effect is caused by a below-chance decoding accuracy in the non-tinnitus group.
evidence: Summary of key finding from both studies.

claim: The original notion of a more generally enhanced prediction score in tinnitus individuals is likely too simplistic.
source: This indicates that our original notion of a more generally enhanced prediction score in tinnitus individuals is likely too simplistic.
evidence: Inference from data patterns.

claim: Further studies using complementary methods and designs will be needed to better understand the predictive processing effect in tinnitus.
source: We have offered some speculations, however, further studies using complementary methods and designs will be needed to better understand this effect.
evidence: Recommendation for future research.
